posts.title: The case for a slower morning
posts.excerpt: Twenty minutes with no screen changed how the rest of my day feels. Here is what I do and what I skipped.
body: For years my mornings began with a phone in one hand and a kettle in the other. The kettle always lost. Somewhere in the scroll the water went cold, and the day started on someone else's schedule.
Now the first twenty minutes belong to me. I boil water, open the window, and write three lines in a notebook: what I am looking forward to, what is worrying me, and one small thing I will finish.
It is not a productivity trick. Nothing gets optimised. I simply arrive at my desk already knowing where I stand, and that turns out to be most of what I wanted from a routine.

posts.title: Seven notes on brewing better tea
posts.excerpt: Water temperature, a quick rinse and a kinder ratio will improve almost any cup. A short list from my kitchen.
body: Start with the water. Green teas prefer it well below boiling, around 80°C, while black and herbal teas can take it fresh off the boil. Hot water on delicate leaves is the quickest route to a bitter cup.
Measure the leaf. A level teaspoon per cup is a fine start, but weigh it once and you will see how much a heaped spoon varies. Two grams per 200 ml is a steady place to begin.
Rinse, steep, taste. A quick rinse wakes the leaf, and tasting at the two-minute mark teaches you more than any timer. Stop when it is where you like it, not when the clock says so.

posts.title: What a notebook can do that an app can't
posts.excerpt: Paper has no notifications, no sync errors and no opinion about your formatting. That is the point.
body: I have tried every notes app. They are all good, and I have lost something in each of them: a half-formed idea, a list, a whole Tuesday. The notebook on my desk has never lost anything because it has never been closed by accident.
Paper also forces small decisions. You cannot move a paragraph, so you think before you write it. Crossings out stay visible, which makes it easy to see how an idea changed.
I still keep an app for anything I need to search. But for thinking I reach for the pen, and the pages are slowly turning into a map of the year.

posts.title: A week of walking to work
posts.excerpt: Forty minutes each way, no headphones. What I noticed and what I stopped carrying.
body: The route is 3.5 kilometres, which takes forty minutes at an unhurried pace. On Monday I took my headphones out of habit. By Wednesday I left them at home and started hearing the street.
Walking turned out to be the best meeting of my week. Problems that felt tangled at my desk loosened somewhere near the bridge, and I began carrying a small notebook to catch them.
I stopped carrying a heavy bag, too. A water bottle, a wallet, keys and a book. Everything else turned out to be optional.

posts.title: How I plan a trip on a single page
posts.excerpt: One sheet, four boxes, and a rule about leaving the afternoons empty.
body: Every trip I have over-planned ended with a spreadsheet I never opened. Now I use one page divided into four boxes: where we sleep, how we move, what we must see, and what we might do.
The must-see box holds three things at most. If we manage them, the trip was a success and everything else is a bonus. This takes the pressure off in a way a long itinerary never does.
The rule I like best is to leave every afternoon empty. The best meals and the strangest conversations of my travels have happened in the gaps.

posts.title: Small rules for a tidy desk
posts.excerpt: Five habits that keep a workspace calm without turning it into a showroom.
body: A tidy desk is not about looking organised. It is about starting each task without having to move something first. I keep only what I used today within arm's reach.
The rules are simple. One cup, one notebook, one pen that works. Cables go behind, not across. Anything that lands on the desk gets a home or leaves by Friday.
Fridays end with a two-minute reset. Wipe the surface, return the cups, close the tabs. Monday's version of me is always grateful.
